items.title: Mike Vax interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 29, 2022
items.q: then in college Gordon Finlay, who’d been the solo cornetist with the Navy band in Washington for 20 years. I studied with him.

ctx.x: I mean that’s so true. And it’s an interesting phenomenon I guess. There are some people, like Wayne was really a natural from the beginning. I was sort of a natural but I wasn’t one of those guys that just had it when I was young. And I had to work really hard to get where some other trumpet players already were, you know in high school and stuff and junior high even. And so I just — I had decided probably by the time I was 14 or 15 I want to be a trumpet player. You know? Just I want to be a trumpet player. And…

still alive, Norm Tompach, who really got me into the jazz thing. He had written for Basie and Woody and he was the leader of the Fort Ord Army Band at one point. And so he was important and then in college Gordon Finlay, who’d been the solo cornetist with the Navy band in Washington for 20 years. I studied with him. And these people made me work. You know I practiced a lot and I practiced what they wanted me to. I didn’t just sit and play tunes or whatever, although I did that afterwards. In fact even when I was…

If you’re playing two different charts and on one chart you have to end on a G above the staff, a high G, and it happens to be the root of the chord. And then the next tune you have to end on that same high G but in this case it’s like it’s a very thick chord, a 13 chord or something and your note is definitely not the root, is the second G harder to play than the first one?
